text:
Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is allowed on a flight in the US, as long as it goes in your carry-on.

**Why it qualifies**
- The FAA limits spare lithium-ion batteries and power banks to 100 watt-hours (Wh) each. To convert, divide mAh by 1000 to get Ah, then multiply by the voltage ([FAA: Airline Passengers and Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries)).
- Most power banks use 3.7 V cells, so 20 Ah × 3.7 V ≈ 74 Wh. That's well under 100 Wh. The 3.7 V figure is my assumption, so check the Wh printed on your unit's label if it has one.

**Rules to follow**
- **Carry-on only.** Spare lithium batteries and power banks are not allowed in checked bags ([FAA: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7)).
- **Gate-checked bags.** If your carry-on is checked at the gate, take the power bank out and keep it with you in the cabin.
- **Protect the terminals.** Keep it in its retail packaging, a pouch, or with the ports covered so nothing shorts against metal.
- **Don't bring a damaged or recalled unit.** Tell the crew right away if a battery gets hot, swollen, or smokes.
- **Airline limits.** The FAA notes that many airlines set stricter limits on the number of power banks or the Wh per passenger, so check your carrier's policy before you fly. International flights may have extra rules, such as limits on use during the flight ([IATA guidance](https://www.iata.org/en/youandiata/travelers/batteries/)).

Power banks over 100 Wh (up to 160 Wh) need airline approval, and you're limited to two. Anything over 160 Wh isn't allowed on passenger aircraft ([FAA PackSafe](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe?packsafeq=power+bank)).
